concepts.name: Model cascading: small model first, escalate when needed
Prompt caching: the prefix, the prices and what breaks it
Estimating monthly cost from token counts

questions.prompt: In a model cascade, what decides whether a query goes to the larger, more expensive model?

choices.text: Every query goes to both models, and the cheaper of the two answers is returned
The small model answers first, and a scorer or validator on its answer decides whether to escalate
The large model handles the first turn of each conversation, and the small model handles the rest
Traffic is split at random, and the split is tuned until the bill is low enough

questions.explanation: A cascade tries cheaper models first and escalates only when the answer fails a check, so most easy queries never touch the expensive model. The FrugalGPT paper describes the cascade as learning which combination of models to use for each query. Calling both models on every query doubles cost instead of cutting it.

sources.title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
sources.claim: FrugalGPT is an LLM cascade that learns which combinations of LLMs to use for different queries to cut cost and improve accuracy.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform
sources.claim: Instead of sending every query to an expensive model, simpler queries can be routed to cheaper models.

questions.prompt: When does a small-model-first cascade fail to save money?

choices.text: When most queries end up escalated, so you pay for the small call and the large call
When the small model is more than 10× cheaper than the large one
When the escalation check is a cheap rule instead of another model call
When most queries are simple, such as greetings and FAQ lookups

questions.explanation: Expected cost per query is roughly the small model's cost plus the escalation rate times the large model's cost (plus the check). If nearly everything escalates, you pay more than calling the large model directly, and latency is worse too. Cascades pay off when most traffic is easy and the price gap is large.

sources.title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
sources.claim: A cascade saves cost by sending queries to cheaper LLMs first and only some to expensive ones, matching GPT-4 performance with up to 98% cost reduction; the saving depends on how many queries need the expensive model.

questions.prompt: Design a model cascade for project 1's support bot. What is the escalation signal, and how would you show it saves money without hurting quality?

model_answer.summary: Answer with a small model, escalate to the large one when an automatic check fails, and prove it on an eval set by comparing quality and cost per conversation with and without the cascade.
key_points: The small model answers first; a concrete check decides escalation, such as output validation failing, a grader or confidence score below a threshold, or an intent known to be hard
Expected cost is about small-model cost plus escalation rate times large-model cost, so the escalation rate is the number to watch
Run the same eval set through large-model-only and the cascade, and compare pass rate and cost
Watch added latency for escalated queries, which pay for two calls
In production, track escalation rate and quality over time, since traffic changes

questions.explanation: An answer is strong when the escalation signal is something you can actually compute and the claim of savings is backed by a measurement, not a hope. Chip Huyen's platform post describes routing simple queries to cheaper models; the cascade adds a check after the cheap attempt.

sources.title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
sources.claim: An LLM cascade chooses per query which models to call, and its benefit is measured as cost versus accuracy against the best single model.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform
sources.claim: A model router can send simpler queries to cheaper models to cut cost.

questions.prompt: Every request to Claude sends the same tool definitions, then a 3,000-token system prompt with a `cache_control` breakpoint at its end. To help the model, you add the current time (to the second) as the first line of the system prompt. What happens to caching?

choices.text: Nothing changes: the cache ignores short lines that differ between requests
Only the tools are cached now, but the system prompt still hits the cache
The cache still hits, but its lifetime drops to one minute
The system prompt's prefix changes on every request, so its cache never hits

questions.explanation: The cache matches an exact prefix, built in the order tools, then system, then messages; any change at a level invalidates that level and everything after it. A timestamp at the top of the system prompt makes each request's prefix unique. Put content that changes after the last cache breakpoint, for example in the user message.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: The cache prefix is built in the order tools, system, messages, and a change at a level invalidates that level and all later levels, so varying text early in the system prompt prevents system-level hits.

questions.prompt: On Anthropic's API with the default 5-minute cache, how are cached tokens priced for most Claude models, relative to the base input price?

choices.text: Cache writes are free and cache reads cost 0.5× base
Cache writes cost 2× base and cache reads cost 0.25× base
Cache writes cost 1.25× base and cache reads cost 0.1× base
Cache writes cost 1× base and cache reads are free

questions.explanation: A 5-minute cache write costs 1.25× the base input price and a cache read 0.1×; the 1-hour cache costs 2× to write. So caching pays off as soon as a prefix is read even once more within the TTL, and each hit refreshes the TTL at no cost. Some of the newest models have even cheaper reads (for example 0.05× on Claude Opus 5.5), so check the pricing table for your model.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: 5-minute cache writes cost 1.25x base input, 1-hour writes 2x, reads 0.1x (0.05x on Claude Opus 5.5), and each use refreshes the cache at no extra cost.

questions.prompt: You mark an 800-token system prompt with `cache_control` on Claude Sonnet 4.6. The request succeeds, but `usage` shows `cache_creation_input_tokens: 0` and `cache_read_input_tokens: 0` on every call. Why?

choices.text: Caching only starts after the same prompt has been sent 10 times
The prompt is under Sonnet 4.6's minimum cacheable length of 1,024 tokens
System prompts can't be cached; only tool definitions and messages can
The cache was written, but `usage` only reports it for streaming requests

questions.explanation: Each model has a minimum cacheable prompt length: 1,024 tokens for Sonnet 4.6, and 512 to 4,096 for other models. Shorter prefixes are simply not cached, and the API returns no error, so check both cache counters in `usage` to confirm caching works.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: Claude Sonnet 4.6's minimum cacheable length is 1,024 tokens (others 512 to 4,096); shorter prompts are processed without caching and no error, leaving both cache usage counters at 0.

questions.prompt: You consider a semantic cache: if a new question's embedding is close enough to a past question, return the past answer. What is the main risk?

choices.text: Questions that are close in embedding space but differ in meaning get a wrong cached answer
It can only store answers shorter than the embedding model's context window
Every cache hit costs more than calling the model would have
It invalidates the provider's prompt cache for all later requests

questions.explanation: "Cancel my order" and "don't cancel my order" can be close in embedding space. A semantic cache depends on good embeddings, reliable vector search and a well-chosen similarity threshold, and a mistake returns a confident wrong answer. Chip Huyen calls its value "more dubious" than exact caching for this reason.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform
sources.claim: Semantic caching's value is more dubious than other caching because it depends on good embeddings, vector search and a similarity metric, and a wrong similarity match returns an incorrect response.

questions.prompt: You re-index your document store every night, and about 95% of chunks haven't changed. How should you cache embeddings so you pay only for what changed?

choices.text: Key the cache on the document's file name, so renamed files are re-embedded
Key the cache on the chunk text alone, and keep it when you switch embedding models
Key the cache on a hash of the chunk text plus the embedding model name
Skip caching: re-embedding everything nightly is the only way to stay consistent

questions.explanation: Embedding the same text with the same model gives a reusable vector, so a hash of (chunk text, model) is a safe key: unchanged chunks hit, edited chunks miss. A file-name key misses edits to a file whose name didn't change. Including the model matters because vectors from different embedding models are not comparable, so a model change must invalidate the cache.

sources.title: Embedding model integrations - Docs by LangChain
sources.claim: CacheBackedEmbeddings keys the cache on a hash of the text and needs a namespace (such as the model name) to avoid collisions when the same text is embedded with different models.

questions.prompt: You run a nightly job that scores 20,000 transcripts with Claude, and nobody waits for the results. Which statement about Anthropic's Message Batches API is true?

choices.text: Usage costs 90% less, and every batch is guaranteed to finish within 5 minutes
Prices are unchanged; the only benefit is separate, higher rate limits for the batch job
Usage costs 50% less, but prompt caching discounts can't be combined with it
Usage costs 50% less; most batches finish within an hour, but can take up to 24 hours

questions.explanation: All batch usage is charged at 50% of standard prices. Most batches complete in under an hour, but a batch that isn't done after 24 hours expires. Batch and prompt-caching discounts stack, though cache hits are best-effort in a batch. A batch holds up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, and results can be downloaded for 29 days.

sources.title: Batch processing
sources.claim: All batch usage costs 50% of standard prices, most batches finish within an hour but expire if not done in 24 hours, caching discounts stack with cache hits best-effort, batches hold up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, and results stay available 29 days.

questions.prompt: Which parts of project 1 would you move to a batch API, which must stay real-time, and what else would you trim to cut cost?

model_answer.summary: Anything no user is waiting for (evals, nightly re-scoring, backfills, bulk summaries) goes to the batch API at half price; the live chat stays real-time, and every prompt is trimmed.
key_points: Batch fits jobs where results can wait hours, such as eval runs, nightly classification or summarisation, and backfills
The live conversation must stay real-time, because a batch can take up to 24 hours
Batch usage is billed at 50% of standard prices, and it can be combined with prompt caching
Trimming cuts tokens on every call: drop or summarise old turns, send only the top retrieved chunks, and remove unused tool definitions and verbose instructions
Measure tokens per call before and after trimming, and check on the eval set that quality holds

questions.explanation: The deciding question for batch is "is anyone waiting?" The deciding question for trimming is "does the model need this to answer?" Both show up directly in the token counts you log.

sources.title: Batch processing
sources.claim: The Batches API suits requests that don't need immediate responses such as evaluations, bills at 50% of standard prices, can take up to 24 hours, and supports prompt caching with stacking discounts.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: Usage reports cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens and input_tokens, which lets you measure tokens per call.

questions.prompt: A conversation has 6 model calls. Each call averages 2,000 input tokens and 300 output tokens. At a hypothetical $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, what do 100,000 conversations a month cost?

choices.text: About $630
About $2,700
About $6,300
About $63,000

questions.explanation: Per conversation: input is 6 × 2,000 = 12,000 tokens × $3/M = $0.036; output is 6 × 300 = 1,800 tokens × $15/M = $0.027. That's $0.063 per conversation, and × 100,000 = $6,300 a month. $2,700 is the output cost alone; the other two are off by a factor of 10. Note that input dominates, which is why caching and trimming matter.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: Pricing is per million tokens of input and output (for example $4/MTok base input on Opus 5.5); worked by hand: 6 x 2,000 x $3/M + 6 x 300 x $15/M = $0.063 per conversation, x 100,000 = $6,300.

questions.prompt: This Lesson's exercise: explain how you would estimate project 1's monthly cost at 1,000 and at 100,000 conversations, and which costs grow differently from the model bill.

model_answer.summary: Measure tokens per conversation from real traces, multiply by prices and volume, then add infrastructure; model cost scales linearly with conversations while some infrastructure is a fixed floor.
key_points: Get average calls per conversation and input and output tokens per call from logs or traces, not guesses
Model cost per conversation is input tokens × input price plus output tokens × output price, adjusted for cached tokens at their cached price
Multiply by monthly conversations: the model bill grows linearly, so 100,000 conversations cost about 100× what 1,000 do
Infrastructure such as an always-on container, a database and monitoring is a fixed monthly floor that dominates at low volume
Embeddings, retrieval and any reranking calls are extra per-conversation costs to include

questions.explanation: At 1,000 conversations the fixed hosting cost often exceeds the model bill; at 100,000 the model bill dominates, and that's where caching, cascading and trimming pay off. Stating both regimes shows you understand where the money goes.

sources.title: Prompt caching
sources.claim: Cached tokens are billed at different multipliers (writes 1.25x or 2x, reads 0.1x) and reported separately in usage, so cost estimates must price cached tokens separately.

sources.title: Building A Generative AI Platform
sources.claim: A generative AI platform includes components beyond the model call, such as retrieval, vector search and caching, each with its own cost.
